## ARGUMENT

**[Officer] Is Entitled to Qualified Immunity Because No Clearly Established Law Prohibited Using a Taser on an Actively Resisting Suspect.**

**A. Plaintiff must identify precedent that placed the question beyond debate.**

Once an officer raises qualified immunity, the plaintiff must show both a constitutional violation and that the right was clearly established when the officer acted. *See Baynes v. Cleland*, 799 F.3d 600, 610 (6th Cir. 2015). The Court may resolve the claim on the second element alone. *Pearson v. Callahan*, 555 U.S. 223, 236 (2009). A right is clearly established only if its contours are "sufficiently clear that a reasonable official would understand that what he is doing violates that right." *Anderson v. Creighton*, 483 U.S. 635, 640 (1987). Although a case directly on point is not required, existing precedent must place the question beyond debate. *Ashcroft v. al-Kidd*, 563 U.S. 731, 741 (2011). The right must therefore be established in a particularized sense, not merely as a general guarantee against excessive force. *See Dorsey v. Barber*, 517 F.3d 389, 394 (6th Cir. 2008). The question is whether precedent existing on [date of incident] would have told every reasonable officer that using a taser on a suspect who was [describe resistance] was unlawful.

**B. This Court's precedent supports taser use against active resistance.**

It would not have. In *Hagans v. Franklin County Sheriff's Office*, 695 F.3d 505 (6th Cir. 2012), a deputy repeatedly applied a taser to a suspect who resisted being handcuffed. This Court held that the deputy was entitled to qualified immunity because, as of May 2007, no clearly established law prohibited that use of a taser on an actively resisting suspect. *Id.* at 508–11. In reaching that conclusion, the Court distinguished force used against compliant or subdued individuals from force used against those who continued to resist. *Id.* at 509–10.

Later decisions confirm the line. *Rudlaff v. Gillispie*, 791 F.3d 638 (6th Cir. 2015), involved an arrestee who resisted officers during a traffic stop and was subjected to a knee strike and a single taser application. The Court reversed the denial of qualified immunity, explaining that officers may use a taser to subdue a suspect who is actively resisting arrest, but not one who is not resisting or has stopped. *Id.* at 641–44.

*Smith v. City of Troy*, 874 F.3d 938 (6th Cir. 2017) (per curiam), likewise affirmed summary judgment where officers used a taser on a suspect who resisted their efforts to handcuff him. *Id.* at 944–45. And in *Roell v. Hamilton County*, 870 F.3d 471 (6th Cir. 2017), deputies used a taser while attempting to restrain a physically resistant man exhibiting signs of excited delirium. The Court affirmed judgment for the deputies, concluding that the plaintiff had not shown a violation of clearly established law. *See id.* at 482–87.

**C. Cases protecting non-resisting suspects cannot carry Plaintiff's burden.**

Plaintiff may invoke *Kent v. Oakland County*, 810 F.3d 384 (6th Cir. 2016), which denied qualified immunity to a deputy who used a taser on a man who, on the facts viewed in his favor, was not actively resisting. *Id.* at 391–97. *Kent* addresses a materially different situation. A precedent forbidding such force against a non-resisting person does not notify an officer that it is forbidden against someone who is [describe resistance]. The line between resistance and nonresistance defeats this claim. *See Rudlaff*, 791 F.3d at 641–44.

Here, [Plaintiff] actively resisted by [facts with record citations]. [Officer] deployed the taser [number and duration of applications, and when use ceased]. *Hagans*, *Rudlaff*, *Smith*, and *Roell* would not have alerted a reasonable officer that this response was unlawful; to the contrary, they support it. Because Plaintiff cannot identify authority clearly establishing otherwise, [Officer] is entitled to qualified immunity and summary judgment on the Fourth Amendment claim.
